title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This is a case of a model asserting false information as fact, specifically a legal AI tool generating nonexistent case citations, fabricated quotes, and false legal holdings that were then submitted to a court without verification. The failure happened at the output-review stage of deployment: a lawyer used the tool under the mistaken belief that it performed citation checks, meaning no independent verification of the generated references was carried out before the filings were submitted. Seven citations across eight filings did not exist.

The failure mode is straightforward hallucination, a well-documented behavior in which generative AI produces plausible-sounding but fabricated content. It was caught not by the filing attorneys but by the opposing side or the court, which is the worst point in a legal workflow for such an error to surface. A routine manual check of each cited case against an authoritative legal database before filing would have been sufficient to catch it.

What is not established is whether the AI tool itself was marketed as performing citation verification, whether the law firm had formal policies governing AI use in filings, or what consequences the court will impose on the attorneys involved.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for using artificial intelligence tools that generated fake legal cases, false quotes, and nonexistent legal holdings in court filings for a lawsuit in Los Angeles. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm after a 2020 fire in her Carson home made it uninhabitable. While repairs were underway, storm damage occurred, and after delays in getting State Farm's approval, the work was never completed. Meni-Siliga and her husband exhausted their savings, declared bankruptcy, and lost their home to foreclosure. The case is scheduled for trial in October.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions, mistakenly believing it performed citation checks. She confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel accepted responsibility for the filings. The incident highlights growing concerns about AI use in law firms, with 41% of law firms and 47% of corporate legal departments now using generative AI. A database tracking legal hallucinations worldwide has documented 1,922 cases, mostly in the United States.
